title: Malavika Mohanan's Banarasi Sari Puts Varanasi's Centuries-Old Kadwa Weaving in Focus
excerpt: The actor's 18th-century-inspired Banarasi, woven in the kadwa technique in which each motif is made separately on the loom, is drawing attention to the Varanasi handloom families behind the craft.
body:
• Malavika Mohanan's Banarasi sari, reported by Vogue India and described by Mathrubhumi English as 18th-century-inspired with intricate kadwa weaving, has put Varanasi's handloom craft in the spotlight.
  • In kadwa weaving, each motif is woven separately on the loom, leaving a clean reverse side with no long floats of thread between motifs.
  • A Banarasi sari can take from 15 days to six months to complete depending on the design, and the craft carries a Geographical Indication tag secured in 2009.
  • Reader check: a genuine handloom Banarasi carries Silk Mark or GI documentation, and kadwa pieces show a clean finish on the reverse rather than cut threads.

A sari worn by actor Malavika Mohanan has become a lesson in how a Banarasi is made. Vogue India reported that her Banarasi sari shines a light on a centuries-old weaving technique from Varanasi, and Mathrubhumi English described the same look as an 18th-century-inspired Banarasi sari with intricate kadwa weaving. The garment's subject is not surface embroidery: the pattern is built into the cloth on the loom itself.

What kadwa weaving actually is

Banarasi saris are woven in Varanasi from finely woven silk with gold and silver brocade, known as zari, according to the Banarasi sari reference. In the kadwa technique, each motif is woven separately with its own supplementary weft, rather than the pattern thread travelling across the full width of the fabric. That is why the reverse of a kadwa piece finishes cleanly, with no long floats connecting one motif to the next, while the faster cutwork method leaves small cut ends where the travelling thread was trimmed.

The motifs themselves draw on a vocabulary built over centuries: intertwining floral and foliate patterns, kalga and bel paisley forms, jaal net-like patterns and mina work. Depending on the intricacy of the design, a single sari can take from 15 days to a month, and sometimes up to six months, to complete.

A craft shaped by migration and courts

Weaving in Banaras was already a thriving textile trade in the late 16th century. Silk brocade weaving is thought to have taken hold after silk weavers migrated from Gujarat during the famine of 1603, and the craft developed through the 18th and 19th centuries, shaped by Mughal-era brocade work in gold and silver threads and by Persian-origin weaver families who settled in the region. The handloom silk industry around Varanasi, spanning districts including Chandauli, Bhadohi, Jaunpur and Azamgarh, has been associated with about 1.2 million people directly or indirectly.

That heritage now has legal protection. In 2009, weaver associations secured Geographical Indication rights for Banaras brocades and saris, which means no sari made outside the six identified districts of Uttar Pradesh can legally be sold as a Banaras sari. The protection matters because the handloom sector has lost ground for years to mechanised units producing similar-looking saris faster and cheaper, and to synthetic alternatives to silk.

"Growing up in a household of artistic parents who loved crafts and textiles, I used to visit cottage industries, with handloom and handicrafts exhibitions. Because of this, I also have a love affair with handloom Saris — cotton, ikat, you name it."

— Malavika Mohanan, in Manifest Magazine

Why her wearing it lands

Mohanan's attachment to handloom is on record. The Kerala-born, Mumbai-bred actor, daughter of cinematographer K. U. Mohanan, told Manifest Magazine that she reaches for silk saris when she wants to feel closer to her roots, and her festive dressing has repeatedly centred the weave rather than surface embellishment. Bollywood Hungama recently documented her in a magenta-pink silk saree with repeating gold elephant motifs and ornate zari borders, styled with traditional gold jewellery and understated makeup.

For buyers in the diaspora

The attention cuts both ways: celebrity visibility raises demand, and demand raises the volume of imitations sold to wedding shoppers abroad. The practical checks follow from how the cloth is made. Turn the sari over — a kadwa Banarasi shows a clean reverse with no long thread floats between motifs. Ask for Silk Mark certification and GI documentation confirming the sari was woven within the Varanasi production zone. And weigh the time honestly: a handwoven piece that took weeks on a loom cannot be priced like a powerloom copy produced in days. Buying the real thing is the most direct way readers abroad can keep Varanasi's weaver families on their looms.
